title: Pier Giorgio Frassati (1901–1925)
hook: a mountain-climbing student who quietly served Turin's poor

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gianna Beretta Molla, who skied and painted and made house calls. Your line was a doctor and a mother. Who did you check on? Today, another saint who loved the mountains. Day nine hundred sixteen.

A funeral in Turin, and the family is confused. The young man in the coffin was the son of a rich and well-known household. They expected the city's important people. They did not expect the streets to fill with the poor: widows, old men, families from the back alleys, people the family had never seen. They had come, one after another, to say that this young man had brought them food, coal, medicine and rent money, quietly, for years. His family hadn't known. That is how the Frassatis learned who their son, Pier Giorgio, had been.
screen: `A FUNERAL IN TURIN.` → `THE POOR FILL THE STREETS.` → `HIS FAMILY HADN'T KNOWN.`

segments.voice: The mountains come first. Pier Giorgio loved the mountains. He hiked and climbed with friends in the Alps, laughing, singing, playing pranks. On one photo of himself on a climb he wrote a short Italian phrase: verso l'alto, to the heights. Second, the student. He studied engineering, and tradition says he chose mining so he could work beside miners, among the hardest-working poor he knew. He went to daily Mass, prayed the rosary, and threw himself into Catholic student groups and politics. Third, the hidden work. Through the Saint Vincent de Paul Society he visited the poor in their homes, week after week. He gave away his money, his coat, his tram fare, and then ran home to be on time for dinner. He didn't tell his parents. Fourth, the end. He fell ill suddenly with polio and died within days, still a young man. Tradition says he caught it from the sick he visited. Even in his last hours, he sent a note asking a friend to bring medicine to a poor man he could no longer reach. The Psalm says, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me." For Pier Giorgio, those who knew him said, climbing was a way of praying. And back in the city there were other climbs: the stairs up to the rooms of the poor. The Church has now canonized him. To the heights meant both: the peak, and the poor man's attic.
screen: `VERSO L'ALTO.` · `A STUDENT WHO CHOSE THE MINES.` · `HIDDEN WORK, WEEK AFTER WEEK.` · `A NOTE FROM HIS DEATHBED.` · then, large: `I HAVE LIFTED UP MY EYES TO THE MOUNTAINS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: go climb something. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture the climb that's within your reach today: a hill, a trail, a park, a flight of stairs at work. Feel your legs ready for it. Now add Pier Giorgio's second half: who is at the top of a staircase near you, someone you could visit or bring something to? Hold both, the climb and the person. If you pray, you can lift your eyes, the way the psalm does. The bell holds the time.
Pier Giorgio Frassati. A young man from Turin who climbed mountains, studied engineering, and quietly served the poor, honored by the Church as a saint.
Your line: to the heights. Today, climb something, even a staircase, and on the way, do one quiet good thing nobody will hear about. Day nine hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Some young Catholics name Pier Giorgio Frassati as a patron, and Catholic youth groups and campus ministries organize hikes and climbs in his memory, sometimes under his phrase verso l'alto.
